legacy_source: SESSIONS_DB SQLite sessions, session_events, and approvals tables

backfill.note: Inserts SQLite-only rows into app_sessions, then app_session_events, then app_approvals, in that foreign-key order. Idempotent and insert-only: ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING, no update path and no delete path, so a row present in both stores but disagreeing is reported as a parity failure rather than overwritten, because PostgreSQL may hold the newer value. Rows the target schema cannot accept are reported with a reason code and never forced: seq <= 0 against CHECK (seq > 0), an event whose session row exists in neither store, a duplicate or already-held (tenant_id, drawing_id), a NULL in a target NOT NULL column, and a consumed-but-undecided approval against CHECK (NOT consumed OR decided). THE COMMAND PATH IS ABSOLUTE ON PURPOSE: deploy/Dockerfile.app COPYs the script to /app/scripts/ but its final WORKDIR is /app/server, so naming the script by the repository-relative path resolves in the image to /app/server/scripts/ and does not exist. That shorter form still works from a source checkout run at the repository root; inside the image only the absolute /app/scripts path does. server/tests/test_postgres_container_wiring.py::test_documented_authority_commands_resolve_in_the_image pins this against the Dockerfile's final WORKDIR and COPY target, for EVERY authority command whose script the Dockerfile copies rather than this one alone, so do not 'tidy' the absolute path away. STAGING IS NOT A VALID PLACE TO RUN THIS, measured 2026-08-06. Staging task definition leaf-platform-app-alt:27 sets no SESSIONS_DB, so the legacy source is the task-local server/sessions.db and dies with the task; production leaf-automation-production-platform:98 DOES set SESSIONS_DB=/data/state/sessions.db on EFS. That is drift, not design. The consequence is a catch-22 rather than a sequencing problem: the only copy the command could do useful work on lives inside the currently running task, the script reaches a container only through an image build, ECS Exec is disabled, and a separate run-task gets its own writable layer and cannot read another task's filesystem. Every delivery path therefore destroys the source before the command can read it. This command is load-bearing in PRODUCTION, where the source is durable and survives the deploy that delivers the tool. Not yet run there either: no deploy was dispatched by the lane that wrote it. DEPLOYMENT ORDER IS LOAD-BEARING: staging leaves SESSIONS_DB unset, so the legacy source is the task-local server/sessions.db rather than the EFS /data/state volume, and the image is built without it. Deploying the image that carries this command therefore replaces the task and destroys the very source the backfill exists to read, after which every row PostgreSQL retained from BEFORE the deploy classifies as an expected target-only row with no surviving source row to contradict it, and the command is expected to report success without recovering anything (rows written after the deploy land in both stores and match normally, and a fresh post-commit mirror failure is still reported, so that clean result is expected rather than guaranteed). Preserve or export the running task's database BEFORE task replacement, or accept that staging's pre-deploy session history is not recoverable and record that instead. DECIDED 2026-08-06 FOR STAGING ONLY: DISCARD, do not preserve, accepting real loss. Dual-write is NOT fail-closed and this decision does not rest on any claim that it is: the legacy write COMMITS FIRST in session_store.get_or_create_session, append_event and create_approval (each calls its _legacy_ writer before its _pg_ mirror; turn acquire/release and approval decide/consume share the shape) and an unwrapped mirror exception cannot roll it back, so a post-commit pre-mirror failure leaves a source-only row, as test_reconcile_sessions_authority.py documents. _pg_ensure_started and the mirror pre-checks narrow that window, they do not close it. Separately, checkpoints.py and session_policy.py put session_checkpoints and session_policies in the SAME file with no PostgreSQL mirror and no coverage here, so preserving the file would not let this command recover them anyway; under the task-local configuration measured here any task replacement destroys them, which is a property of the current configuration forward rather than a checked history of earlier revisions. What bounds the accepted loss is that the file starts empty at task start and the running task carried dual_write_shadow for its whole life, so exposure is one task-lifetime of staging traffic. Consequence to carry forward: the first staging backfill is EXPECTED to insert nothing, and that expected-empty result is indistinguishable from the post-deploy false-clean, so read it as nothing left to read, never as nothing to recover; a clean staging parity run certifies only agreement since the new task started and is NOT evidence of recovery. Rationale in docs/POSTGRES-CUTOVER.md. Staging-only: must not be reused for production, which sets SESSIONS_DB on durable EFS.

parity.note: Full-data comparison of all three table pairs, not a sampled read. Exits 0 only when every legacy row has a matching target row, 1 with a per-table breakdown when parity fails, and 2 when it could not run. Target-only rows are EXPECTED and never a failure WHEN THE SOURCE IS DUAL-WRITING, which is the condition this tolerance was written for and is no longer staging's: staging's LEAF_SESSIONS_STORE is postgres as of 2026-08-13, and session_store._DUAL_WRITE_MODES holds only dual_write and dual_write_shadow, so the SQLite source receives no session writes at all. Against a frozen source and a growing target every new row is target-only and a run reconciles trivially, which is the manufactured-receipt shape described at the end of this note wearing a different face. Read the tolerance as conditional on the mode, never as a property of the environment. Read-only on both stores by enforcement, not by intention: SQLite is opened mode=ro and the PostgreSQL transaction is READ ONLY at repeatable read. Compares parsed JSON (both sides read as text, since psycopg decodes a JSONB string and a JSONB boolean alike), exact floats (REAL vs DOUBLE PRECISION, matching session_store._shadow_equal's bare !=), and INTEGER 0/1 against BOOLEAN without coercion. Also checks the last_seq == max(seq, 0) invariant over every source session, because both stores can hold the SAME broken state and reconcile happily, then collide on the first turn after the flip. A CLEAN RUN IS NOT BY ITSELF A CUTOVER CERTIFICATE: the two stores are snapshotted separately and the app holds no lock across its dual write, so a legacy commit that lands between the halves, or after the source re-read, is invisible to both. The command detects a source that moved under it (source_stable) and narrows that window, but only quiescing legacy writes closes it. Treat writer quiescence as a required prerequisite of the flip transaction, not of this command. AN EMPTY SOURCE AGAINST A POPULATED TARGET NO LONGER EXITS 0. That state reconciles trivially (every target row is an expected target-only row) and proves only that the empty set is a subset, yet it is exactly the shape a destroyed or task-local source takes after a deploy. The command now reports empty_source_populated_target and withholds a clean exit unless --allow-empty-source is passed deliberately, so a cutover receipt cannot be manufactured out of a source that is simply gone. Not yet run against staging: see the backfill note, staging is not a valid place to run it.

authorities.rollback_mode: Return through shadow or dual_write only while single-task, then select legacy after reverse reconciliation. ORDERING IS MANDATORY: every mode on that return path except postgres reads legacy SQLite at SESSIONS_DB, which staging leaves unset, so on staging they all resolve to the task-local server/sessions.db that dies with the task. Any rollback off postgres on staging must set SESSIONS_DB to durable storage in the same transaction, before or with the selector change, never after. The two stores have no atomic transaction. Note that shadow is on the RETURN path, not the way forward: shadow is absent from session_store._DUAL_WRITE_MODES, so it stops mirroring to PostgreSQL entirely. Promote dual_write_shadow straight to postgres and never through shadow.

legacy_source: SESSIONS_DB SQLite session_checkpoints and session_policies tables

backfill.note: NO BACKFILL COMMAND EXISTS FOR THESE TWO TABLES. scripts/reconcile_sessions_authority.py covers exactly three table pairs (sessions/app_sessions, session_events/app_session_events, approvals/app_approvals) and neither annex table is among them, so it must not be cited as this authority's backfill. Selecting any mode other than legacy therefore starts from an EMPTY PostgreSQL target: dual_write mirrors rows written from that moment forward and copies nothing that already exists. WHAT THAT COSTS DEPENDS ENTIRELY ON THE ENVIRONMENT, and the two are opposite cases. On staging SESSIONS_DB is unset, so the legacy source is the task-local server/sessions.db that dies with every task, and no history accumulates ACROSS task replacements. TASK-LOCAL IS NOT EMPTY, and an earlier draft of this record wrongly implied it was (review round 1). The RUNNING task holds up to one task-lifetime of checkpoints and non-default policies, so selecting postgres discards those rows while the mirrored session itself survives, which is the exact user-visible mismatch this authority exists to remove, occurring once at cutover. That is inside the discard class staging already accepted for app_sessions_and_approvals and it is bounded by one task lifetime rather than by history, which is why staging can still select postgres directly and skip the backfill phase. It is a real loss taken knowingly, not an absence of anything to lose. Production sets SESSIONS_DB=/data/state/sessions.db on durable EFS, so its checkpoints and policies HAVE accumulated across task replacements, and cutting production over without first writing a backfill would silently drop every existing restore point and every non-default policy. Write the backfill before production, not before staging. The two tables are independent inserts with no ordering constraint between them and no foreign key to app_sessions (see 0029_session_annex.sql), so a backfill is a simpler shape than the sessions one: no parent-first ordering, no sequence invariant. The cap in checkpoints.CHECKPOINT_CAP is the one thing it must respect, since a source session already holding 50 rows must not become 51 in the target.

parity.note: No parity command exists for these tables either. The in-process substitute is the shadow read: dual_write_shadow and shadow compare every read against PostgreSQL and raise on disagreement (server/session_annex.shadow_equal), which covers rows as they are READ rather than the full table, and only for sessions actually in use. That is weaker than a full-table sweep in two specific ways worth stating: it never examines a row nobody reads, and it does not compare WRITES, because a shadow-mode write deliberately does not reach PostgreSQL and comparing straight after one would test a target the mode chose not to update. Do not record a clean shadow period as a parity certificate.

authorities.rollback_mode: ROLLBACK IS UNDESIGNED AND MUST NOT BE ASSUMED. Returning through shadow or dual_write to legacy makes SQLite the read authority again, and there is no PostgreSQL-to-SQLite writer anywhere in this repository -- scripts/reconcile_sessions_authority.py is SQLite to PostgreSQL only, and it does not cover these tables in either direction. So every checkpoint and policy written while postgres was the authority becomes unreadable the moment the selector leaves postgres, and stays unreadable. ON STAGING that is inside the accepted discard class already recorded for app_sessions_and_approvals: the legacy target is the task-local server/sessions.db, so rollback loses the annex rows whatever anyone does, and the degradation is the safe direction (checkpoint lists read empty, get_policy falls back to DEFAULT_POLICY='confirm_all'). Roll back on staging knowing that, not expecting recovery. ON PRODUCTION it is a blocker, not a caveat, and it is the reason production must not select postgres before a reverse writer exists. Production's SQLite source is durable on EFS, so a rollback there would silently revert every user's restore points to whatever the file held at cutover time while newer PostgreSQL rows survive, unread, in a table nothing consults. Note also that the ordering rule recorded for LEAF_SESSIONS_STORE -- any rollback off postgres on staging must set SESSIONS_DB to durable storage in the same transaction -- applies here identically and for the same reason.
